claim: Tumor cells expressing oncogenic Drosophila Hipk display elevated aerobic glycolysis.
source: Here, we show that in an in vivo tumor model expressing oncogenic Drosophila Homeodomain-interacting protein kinase (Hipk), tumor cells display elevated aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-2 including 2-NBDG uptake assays, glucose FRET measurements, and glycolytic gene expression analysis.

claim: Elevated Hipk drives transcriptional upregulation of Drosophila Myc (dMyc) likely through convergence of multiple perturbed signaling cascades.
source: Mechanistically, elevated Hipk drives transcriptional upregulation of Drosophila Myc (dMyc; MYC in vertebrates) likely through convergence of multiple perturbed signaling cascades.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing dMyc upregulation (Figure 3a), dMyc-lacZ reporter expression (Figure 3c-d), and flip-out clone experiments showing that perturbation of individual signaling pathways (Hippo, Wnt, Hedgehog, Notch) results in dMyc accumulation (Figure 4).

claim: dMyc induces robust expression of pfk2 (encoding 6-Phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase) among other glycolytic genes.
source: dMyc induces robust expression of pfk2 (encoding 6-Phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase; PFKFB in vertebrates) among other glycolytic genes.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data showing that dMyc overexpression leads to upregulation of glycolytic genes including pfk2 (Figure 5e), and that pfk2 is upregulated 2.7-fold in hipk-expressing discs (Figure 2a).

claim: Pfk2 catalyzes the synthesis of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which acts as a potent allosteric activator of Phosphofructokinase (Pfk) and thus stimulates glycolysis.
source: Pfk2 catalyzes the synthesis of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which acts as a potent allosteric activator of Phosphofructokinase (Pfk) and thus stimulates glycolysis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the function of Pfk2 and F2,6-BP in regulating glycolysis, as referenced in the discussion where the authors note 'The allosteric regulation of PFK by F2,6-BP seems to be conserved among mammals and insects as F2,6-BP is able to activate insect Pfk' (Nunes et al., 2016).

claim: Pfk2 and Pfk are required to sustain dMyc protein accumulation post-transcriptionally, establishing a positive feedback loop.
source: Pfk2 and Pfk in turn are required to sustain dMyc protein accumulation post-transcriptionally, establishing a positive feedback loop.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data showing that knockdown of pfk2 or pfk abolishes dMyc protein accumulation (Figure 6a-c) while dMyc transcriptional activation remains robust as shown by dMyc-lacZ reporter (Figure 6e-g), indicating post-transcriptional regulation.

claim: Disruption of the positive feedback loop between dMyc and aerobic glycolysis abrogates tumorous growth.
source: Disruption of the loop abrogates tumorous growth.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that knockdown of dMyc (Figure 5f-i), pfk2 (Figure 6b), or pfk (Figure 6c) in hipk-expressing discs suppresses tumor growth and restores tissue architecture.

claim: Cells with elevated Hipk exhibit statistically significant 2-NBDG accumulation compared to neighboring wild-type cells.
source: Similarly, we found that cells with elevated Hipk (RFP positive) in hipk-expressing wing discs (dpp>RFP +  hipk) exhibited statistically significant 2-NBDG accumulation when compared with the neighboring wild-type cells (RFP negative) (Figure 1c–d and i) or cells (either RFP positive or negative) in control discs (dpp>RFP) (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1i (p = 8.93E-08) and microscopy images in Figure 1c-d showing increased 2-NBDG signal in RFP-positive cells.

claim: A lower FRET/CFP ratio indicative of reduced glucose concentration was observed in hipk-expressing cells compared to control discs.
source: Intriguingly, a lower FRET/CFP ratio indicative of reduced glucose concentration was observed in hipk-expressing cells (Figure 1g–h and k) when compared with control discs (Figure 1e–f and k).
evidence: This is supported by FRET imaging data shown in Figure 1e-h and quantification in Figure 1k (p = 1.04E-08) showing decreased FRET/CFP ratio in hipk-expressing discs.

claim: Despite enhanced glucose uptake, glucose is substantially utilized in the rapidly proliferating Hipk tumor cells.
source: This implies that despite enhanced glucose uptake, glucose is substantially utilized in the rapidly proliferating Hipk tumor cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of increased 2-NBDG uptake (Figure 1c-d, i) and decreased intracellular glucose levels measured by FRET (Figure 1g-h, k).

claim: Genes encoding Hexokinases (Hex-A and Hex-C) are significantly upregulated 2.2-fold and 4.3-fold respectively in hipk-expressing discs.
source: qRT-PCR analyses revealed that genes encoding Hexokinases (Hex-A and Hex-C, 2.2-fold and 4.3-fold respectively), Phosphoglucose isomerase (Pgi, 2.4-fold), Phosphofructokinase 2 (Pfk2, also known as Pfrx, 2.7-fold) and Lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh, also known as Impl3, 3.4-fold) are significantly upregulated in hipk-expressing discs (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This is directly supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2a with statistical significance indicated (p values shown).

claim: Phosphoglucose isomerase (Pgi) is upregulated 2.4-fold in hipk-expressing discs.
source: qRT-PCR analyses revealed that genes encoding Hexokinases (Hex-A and Hex-C, 2.2-fold and 4.3-fold respectively), Phosphoglucose isomerase (Pgi, 2.4-fold), Phosphofructokinase 2 (Pfk2, also known as Pfrx, 2.7-fold) and Lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh, also known as Impl3, 3.4-fold) are significantly upregulated in hipk-expressing discs (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This is directly supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Phosphofructokinase 2 (Pfk2) is upregulated 2.7-fold in hipk-expressing discs.
source: qRT-PCR analyses revealed that genes encoding Hexokinases (Hex-A and Hex-C, 2.2-fold and 4.3-fold respectively), Phosphoglucose isomerase (Pgi, 2.4-fold), Phosphofructokinase 2 (Pfk2, also known as Pfrx, 2.7-fold) and Lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh, also known as Impl3, 3.4-fold) are significantly upregulated in hipk-expressing discs (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This is directly supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh) is upregulated 3.4-fold in hipk-expressing discs.
source: qRT-PCR analyses revealed that genes encoding Hexokinases (Hex-A and Hex-C, 2.2-fold and 4.3-fold respectively), Phosphoglucose isomerase (Pgi, 2.4-fold), Phosphofructokinase 2 (Pfk2, also known as Pfrx, 2.7-fold) and Lactate dehydrogenase (Ldh, also known as Impl3, 3.4-fold) are significantly upregulated in hipk-expressing discs (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This is directly supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2a and confirmed by Ldh-GFP reporter expression in Figure 2c-d.

claim: Robust Ldh-GFP expression was observed in hipk-expressing wing discs.
source: On the contrary, we observed robust Ldh-GFP expression in hipk-expressing wing discs (Figure 2d), confirming that elevated Hipk induces Ldh expression.
evidence: This is directly shown by microscopy images in Figure 2d showing strong GFP signal in hipk-expressing discs compared to minimal signal in control discs (Figure 2c).

claim: glut1 was mildly upregulated 1.6-fold in hipk-expressing discs.
source: Furthermore, we detected a mild upregulation of glut1 (1.6-fold) in hipk-expressing discs by quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Knockdown of glut1 using RNA interference moderately reduced 2-NBDG incorporation in Hipk tumor cells.
source: Knockdown of glut1 using RNA interference (RNAi) moderately reduced 2-NBDG incorporation in Hipk tumor cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c-d comparing 2-NBDG uptake in hipk-expressing discs with and without glut1-RNAi.

claim: dMyc was upregulated in hipk-expressing discs whereas sima expression remained unchanged.
source: qRT-PCR analyses showed that dMyc was upregulated in hipk-expressing discs whereas sima expression remained unchanged (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is directly supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3a with p values indicating statistical significance for dMyc (p = 0.0003) and no significance for sima (p = 0.466).

claim: In control wing discs, dMyc was expressed at high levels in the pouch region.
source: Using a dMyc-lacZ enhancer trap (encoding β-galactosidase (β-gal)) to monitor the transcriptional control of dMyc in vivo, we observed that dMyc was expressed at high levels in the pouch region of control discs (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is shown by β-galactosidase staining in Figure 3c showing strong signal in the pouch region of control discs.

claim: In the hinge and notum areas of control discs, dMyc was minimally and weakly expressed, respectively.
source: In the hinge and notum areas of control discs, dMyc was minimally and weakly expressed, respectively (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is shown by β-galactosidase staining in Figure 3c showing low signal in hinge and notum regions of control discs.

claim: In hipk-expressing discs, intense β-galactosidase staining was found, confirming that Hipk cell-autonomously drives transcriptional upregulation of dMyc.
source: In hipk-expressing discs, we found intense β-galactosidase staining, confirming that Hipk cell-autonomously drives transcriptional upregulation of dMyc.
evidence: This is shown by β-galactosidase staining in Figure 3d showing strong signal in hipk-expressing regions compared to control in Figure 3c.

claim: The increase in β-gal signal intensity appeared to be the largest in the wing hinge where tumor cells proliferated most rapidly.
source: Interestingly, the increase in the β-gal signal intensity appeared to be the largest in the wing hinge (Figure 3d, arrowhead) where the tumor cells proliferated most rapidly, while the intensity faded when moving away from the hinge region (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is shown by β-galactosidase staining in Figure 3d with an arrowhead indicating the strongest signal in the hinge region.

claim: Immunofluorescent staining confirmed the accumulation of dMyc proteins in Hipk tumor cells especially in the wing hinge.
source: Immunofluorescent staining using antibodies against dMyc confirmed the accumulation of dMyc proteins in Hipk tumor cells especially in the wing hinge (Figure 3e–f), which positively correlates with the marked increase in dMyc mRNA levels in the same region (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is shown by dMyc immunostaining in Figure 3f with an arrowhead indicating dMyc accumulation in the hinge region of hipk-expressing discs compared to control in Figure 3e.

claim: dMyc proteins appeared to not accumulate in hipk-expressing cells in the wing pouch.
source: dMyc proteins appeared to not accumulate in hipk-expressing cells in the wing pouch (Figure 3f), possibly due to weak induction in dMyc transcription (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is shown by dMyc immunostaining in Figure 3f showing no obvious increase in dMyc signal in the pouch region of hipk-expressing discs.

claim: hipk-expressing clones located in the dorsal hinge exhibited marked dMyc accumulation.
source: We observed that hipk-expressing clones located in the dorsal hinge (Figure 4c, arrowhead, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), the lateral hinge (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b) as well as the epithelium on the peripodial side exhibited marked dMyc accumulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is shown by dMyc immunostaining in flip-out clones in Figure 4c with arrowhead indicating dMyc accumulation in a dorsal hinge clone.

claim: When hipk-expressing clones were located in the wing pouch, dMyc levels appeared unchanged.
source: On the contrary, when hipk-expressing clones were located in the wing pouch, dMyc levels appeared unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is shown by dMyc immunostaining in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d showing no obvious dMyc accumulation in pouch clones.

claim: Elevated Hipk drives dMyc upregulation in a region-specific manner.
source: Altogether, our data imply that elevated Hipk drives dMyc upregulation in a region-specific manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential dMyc accumulation observed in different regions of the wing disc (hinge vs. pouch) as shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Hipk stimulates the transcriptional activity of Yorkie (Yki), the effector of the Hippo tumor suppressor pathway.
source: For example, Hipk stimulates the transcriptional activity of Yorkie (Yki, a Drosophila orthologue of YAP/TAZ), the effector of the Hippo tumor suppressor pathway (Chen and Verheyen, 2012; Poon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Chen and Verheyen, 2012; Poon et al., 2012).

claim: Hipk functions as a positive regulator of Wnt/Wingless signaling by stabilizing Armadillo.
source: Hipk also functions as a positive regulator of both Wnt/Wingless (Wg) and Hedgehog signaling by stabilizing Armadillo (β-catenin in vertebrates) and Cubitus interruptus (Ci; Gli in vertebrates), respectively (Lee et al., 2009a; Swarup and Verheyen, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Lee et al., 2009a; Swarup and Verheyen, 2011).

claim: Hipk functions as a positive regulator of Hedgehog signaling by stabilizing Cubitus interruptus (Ci).
source: Hipk also functions as a positive regulator of both Wnt/Wingless (Wg) and Hedgehog signaling by stabilizing Armadillo (β-catenin in vertebrates) and Cubitus interruptus (Ci; Gli in vertebrates), respectively (Lee et al., 2009a; Swarup and Verheyen, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Lee et al., 2009a; Swarup and Verheyen, 2011).

claim: Hipk antagonizes Groucho to promote Notch signal transduction.
source: In addition, Hipk has been found to antagonize Groucho, a global co-repressor, to promote Notch signal transduction (Lee et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study (Lee et al., 2009b).

claim: Flip-out clones expressing a constitutively active form of Yki (Yki-S168A) in the dorsal hinge displayed dMyc upregulation.
source: Flip-out clones expressing a constitutively active form of Yki (Yki-S168A) to inactivate the Hippo pathway were usually round and most of them in the dorsal hinge displayed dMyc upregulation (Figure 4d, arrowheads).
evidence: This is shown by dMyc immunostaining in Figure 4d with arrowheads indicating dMyc accumulation in Yki-S168A-expressing clones in the hinge region.

claim: Wing discs with flip-out clones expressing an active form of Arm (Arm-S10) featured an expansion in the hinge area and some dMyc accumulated at the interface between the clone and the neighboring wild-type cells.
source: Wing discs with flip-out clones expressing an active form of Arm (Arm-S10) featured an expansion in the hinge area and some dMyc accumulated at the interface between the clone and the neighboring wild-type cells (Figure 4e, arrowheads) but not at the center of the clone.
evidence: This is shown by dMyc immunostaining in Figure 4e with arrowheads indicating dMyc accumulation at clone boundaries.

claim: Flip-out clones expressing Ci to activate Hedgehog signaling in the hinge region exhibited elevated levels of dMyc.
source: Flip-out clones expressing Ci to activate Hedgehog signaling in the hinge region were round or irregular in shape and exhibited elevated levels of dMyc (Figure 4f, arrowheads).
evidence: This is shown by dMyc immunostaining in Figure 4f with arrowheads indicating dMyc accumulation in Ci-expressing clones in the hinge region.

claim: Expression of activated Notch appeared to induce dMyc accumulation in both cell and non-cell autonomous fashions in the hinge area.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Djiane et al., 2013), expression of activated Notch appeared to induce dMyc accumulation in both cell and non-cell autonomous fashions in the hinge area likely involving a signaling relay (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is shown by dMyc immunostaining in Figure 4g with arrowheads indicating dMyc accumulation in and around N-act-expressing clones, and is consistent with a cited previous study (Djiane et al., 2013).

claim: Individual perturbation of signaling pathways that have been previously shown to be regulated by Hipk was sufficient to trigger ectopic dMyc expression in the hinge region.
source: Therefore, individual perturbation of signaling pathways that have been previously shown to be regulated by Hipk was sufficient to trigger ectopic dMyc expression in the hinge region.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that activation of Yki, Arm, Ci, or Notch individually results in dMyc accumulation in the hinge region (Figure 4d-g).

claim: Overexpression of dMyc caused marked 2-NBDG uptake.
source: As expected and previously reported (de la Cova et al., 2014), overexpression of dMyc caused marked 2-NBDG uptake (Figure 5a and d) and promoted glycolytic gene expression (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is shown by 2-NBDG uptake assay in Figure 5a and quantification in Figure 5d (p = 9.12E-05), and is consistent with a cited previous study (de la Cova et al., 2014).

claim: Overexpression of dMyc promoted glycolytic gene expression.
source: As expected and previously reported (de la Cova et al., 2014), overexpression of dMyc caused marked 2-NBDG uptake (Figure 5a and d) and promoted glycolytic gene expression (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is shown by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5e showing upregulation of glycolytic genes in dMyc-expressing discs, and is consistent with a cited previous study (de la Cova et al., 2014).

claim: Knockdown of dMyc by RNAi in hipk-expressing discs reversed the 2-NBDG accumulation.
source: More importantly, knockdown of dMyc by RNAi in hipk-expressing discs reversed the 2-NBDG accumulation (Figure 5b–d) and moderately suppressed glycolytic gene upregulation (Figure 5e), suggesting that dMyc is essential for the enhanced glycolysis in Hipk tumor cells.
evidence: This is shown by 2-NBDG uptake assay in Figure 5c and quantification in Figure 5d (p = 0.774, not significant) showing that dMyc knockdown prevents 2-NBDG accumulation in hipk-expressing cells.

claim: Knockdown of dMyc in hipk-expressing discs moderately suppressed glycolytic gene upregulation.
source: More importantly, knockdown of dMyc by RNAi in hipk-expressing discs reversed the 2-NBDG accumulation (Figure 5b–d) and moderately suppressed glycolytic gene upregulation (Figure 5e), suggesting that dMyc is essential for the enhanced glycolysis in Hipk tumor cells.
evidence: This is shown by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5e showing reduced glycolytic gene expression in hipk-expressing discs with dMyc knockdown compared to hipk alone.

claim: dMyc is essential for the enhanced glycolysis in Hipk tumor cells.
source: More importantly, knockdown of dMyc by RNAi in hipk-expressing discs reversed the 2-NBDG accumulation (Figure 5b–d) and moderately suppressed glycolytic gene upregulation (Figure 5e), suggesting that dMyc is essential for the enhanced glycolysis in Hipk tumor cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that dMyc knockdown reverses 2-NBDG accumulation and suppresses glycolytic gene expression in hipk-expressing discs (Figure 5b-e).

claim: Knockdown of dMyc significantly suppressed the tumorous growth and tissue distortions in hipk-expressing discs.
source: Additionally, knockdown of dMyc significantly suppressed the tumorous growth and tissue distortions in hipk-expressing discs, as seen by the decrease in GFP positive cells (Figure 5f–g).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy images in Figure 5g showing restored tissue architecture in hipk-expressing discs with dMyc knockdown compared to hipk alone in Figure 5f.

claim: Overexpression of dMyc alone, despite the enhanced glycolysis, failed to reproduce the tumorous phenotypes observed in hipk-expressing discs.
source: Intriguingly, overexpression of dMyc alone (Figure 5a), despite the enhanced glycolysis, failed to reproduce the tumorous phenotypes observed in hipk-expressing discs (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is shown by comparing the tissue morphology in dMyc-expressing discs (Figure 5a) which appears normal, to hipk-expressing discs (Figure 5f) which show severe tissue distortions.

claim: While upregulation of dMyc is indispensable for Hipk-induced glycolysis and tumor growth, additional mechanisms are involved in the Hipk tumors to trigger the tumorigenic process.
source: Thus, while upregulation of dMyc is indispensable for Hipk-induced glycolysis and tumor growth, additional mechanisms are involved in the Hipk tumors to trigger the tumorigenic process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dMyc overexpression alone does not cause tumorous phenotypes (Figure 5a) even though it enhances glycolysis, while dMyc knockdown suppresses Hipk-induced tumors (Figure 5f-g).

claim: Knockdown of pfk2 markedly prevented tumor growth and restored tissue architecture in hipk-expressing discs.
source: Knockdown of pfk2, on the contrary, markedly prevented tumor growth and restored tissue architecture in hipk-expressing discs (Figure 6b), suggesting that the committed step of glycolysis determines Hipk tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is shown by microscopy images in Figure 6b showing restored tissue architecture in hipk-expressing discs with pfk2 knockdown compared to hipk alone in Figure 6a.

claim: The committed step of glycolysis determines Hipk tumorigenesis.
source: Knockdown of pfk2, on the contrary, markedly prevented tumor growth and restored tissue architecture in hipk-expressing discs (Figure 6b), suggesting that the committed step of glycolysis determines Hipk tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that knockdown of pfk2 or pfk, which govern the committed step of glycolysis, effectively suppresses Hipk tumor growth (Figure 6b-c).

claim: The effect of pfk knockdown was comparable to that of pfk2 knockdown in suppressing Hipk tumor growth.
source: Indeed, the effect of pfk knockdown was comparable to that of pfk2 knockdown (Figure 6c), even though we did not detect significant pfk upregulation (<1.5 fold) in hipk-expressing discs (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is shown by comparing microscopy images in Figure 6b (pfk2 knockdown) and Figure 6c (pfk knockdown), both showing restored tissue architecture.

claim: Knockdown of pgk, pyk or Ldh appeared to slightly restrict Hipk tumor growth but the tissue morphology remained distorted.
source: Knockdown of pgk, pyk or Ldh appeared to slightly restrict Hipk tumor growth but the tissue morphology remained distorted (Figure 6d, Figure 6—figure supplement 3c–d).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy images in Figure 6d (Ldh knockdown) and Figure 6—figure supplement 3c-d (pgk and pyk knockdown) showing that tissue distortions persist despite knockdown.

claim: dMyc accumulation was largely abolished in hipk-expressing discs when pfk2 or pfk was knocked down.
source: Intriguingly, dMyc accumulation was largely abolished in hipk-expressing discs when pfk2 or pfk was knocked down (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This is shown by dMyc immunostaining in Figure 6b-c showing loss of dMyc accumulation in hipk-expressing discs with pfk2 or pfk knockdown compared to hipk alone in Figure 6a.

claim: In the absence of hipk overexpression, neither knockdown of pfk nor pfk2 affected the normal dMyc expression pattern nor led to defects in tissue growth.
source: In the absence of hipk overexpression, neither knockdown of pfk nor pfk2 affected the normal dMyc expression pattern nor led to defects in tissue growth (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown by dMyc immunostaining in Figure 6—figure supplement 4a-b showing normal dMyc expression patterns in discs with pfk or pfk2 knockdown alone.

claim: Knockdown of glut1, pgi, pgk, pyk or Ldh in Hipk tumor cells did not rescue dMyc upregulation.
source: Knockdown of glut1, pgi, pgk, pyk or Ldh in Hipk tumor cells did not rescue dMyc upregulation (Figure 6d, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by dMyc immunostaining in Figure 6d and Figure 6—figure supplement 3a-d showing persistent dMyc accumulation in hipk-expressing discs with knockdown of these glycolytic genes.

claim: dMyc accumulation and the associated Hipk tumor growth are most sensitive to the committed step of glycolysis governed by Pfk2-Pfk.
source: Together, our results suggest that dMyc accumulation and the associated Hipk tumor growth are most sensitive to the committed step of glycolysis governed by Pfk2-Pfk.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only knockdown of pfk2 or pfk, but not other glycolytic enzymes, abolishes dMyc accumulation and suppresses tumor growth (Figure 6).

claim: dMyc transcriptional activation remained robust when pfk2 or pfk was depleted in Hipk tumor cells even though the tumor growth was reduced and dMyc protein levels were reduced.
source: Using the dMyc-lacZ reporter, we found that dMyc transcriptional activation remained robust when pfk2 or pfk was depleted in Hipk tumor cells even though the tumor growth was reduced and dMyc protein levels were reduced (Figure 6e–g).
evidence: This is shown by β-galactosidase staining in Figure 6f-g showing strong dMyc-lacZ signal in hipk-expressing discs with pfk2 or pfk knockdown, comparable to hipk alone in Figure 6e.

claim: Pfk2 and Pfk are required to sustain ectopic dMyc expression specifically in Hipk tumor cells through post-transcriptional regulation.
source: Thus, our data indicate that Pfk2 and Pfk are required to sustain ectopic dMyc expression specifically in Hipk tumor cells through post-transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pfk2/pfk knockdown abolishes dMyc protein accumulation (Figure 6b-c) while dMyc transcription remains active (Figure 6f-g), indicating post-transcriptional regulation.

claim: Blocking glycolysis does not trigger Hipk protein degradation.
source: First, we did not detect a noticeable change in Hipk protein levels in discs depleted of pfk2 or pfk when compared with discs expressing hipk alone (Figure 6e–g), indicating that blocking glycolysis does not trigger Hipk protein degradation.
evidence: This is shown by Hipk immunostaining in Figure 6e-g showing comparable Hipk protein levels in hipk-expressing discs with or without pfk2/pfk knockdown.

claim: Hipk activities remain intact when pfk2 or pfk is knocked down.
source: Second, the robust stimulation of the dMyc-lacZ reporter in hipk-expressing discs with pfk2 or pfk knockdown suggests that Hipk activities remain intact.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong dMyc-lacZ signal in hipk-expressing discs with pfk2/pfk knockdown (Figure 6f-g), and is further supported by data showing that Hipk-mediated signaling outputs remain unaffected (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).

claim: Hipk-mediated stabilization of Armadillo remained unaffected by knockdown of pfk2 or pfk.
source: Indeed, when we examined other signaling targets downstream of Hipk as readouts for Hipk activity, we found that Hipk-mediated stabilization of Armadillo (Wnt/Wg signaling), and induction of Cyclin E or expanded-lacZ (Hippo signaling) remained unaffected by knockdown of pfk2 or pfk in a Hipk overexpression background, indicating Hipk is still functional (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown by Armadillo immunostaining in Figure 6—figure supplement 5c-d showing persistent Armadillo stabilization in hipk-expressing discs with pfk2 or pfk knockdown.

claim: Hipk-mediated induction of Cyclin E remained unaffected by knockdown of pfk2 or pfk.
source: Indeed, when we examined other signaling targets downstream of Hipk as readouts for Hipk activity, we found that Hipk-mediated stabilization of Armadillo (Wnt/Wg signaling), and induction of Cyclin E or expanded-lacZ (Hippo signaling) remained unaffected by knockdown of pfk2 or pfk in a Hipk overexpression background, indicating Hipk is still functional (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown by Cyclin E immunostaining in Figure 6—figure supplement 5c-d showing persistent Cyclin E induction in hipk-expressing discs with pfk2 or pfk knockdown.

claim: Hipk-mediated induction of expanded-lacZ remained unaffected by knockdown of pfk2 or pfk.
source: Indeed, when we examined other signaling targets downstream of Hipk as readouts for Hipk activity, we found that Hipk-mediated stabilization of Armadillo (Wnt/Wg signaling), and induction of Cyclin E or expanded-lacZ (Hippo signaling) remained unaffected by knockdown of pfk2 or pfk in a Hipk overexpression background, indicating Hipk is still functional (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown by β-galactosidase staining in Figure 6—figure supplement 5f-g showing persistent expanded-lacZ induction in hipk-expressing discs with pfk2 knockdown.

claim: A positive feedback loop between dMyc and aerobic glycolysis is formed, coordinating growth signals with metabolic states to reinforce tumor progression.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that while dMyc upregulation promotes glycolytic activities, the upregulation of Pfk2, along with subsequent F2,6-BP biosynthesis and Pfk activation, is required to foster the accumulation of dMyc proteins. In other words, a positive feedback loop between dMyc and aerobic glycolysis is formed, coordinating growth signals with metabolic states to reinforce tumor progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that dMyc induces glycolytic gene expression including pfk2 (Figure 5e), and that Pfk2/Pfk are required to sustain dMyc protein accumulation (Figure 6a-c), forming a feedback loop.

claim: Knockdown of pfk2 significantly decreased pyruvate levels.
source: Similarly, knockdown of pfk2 induced an approximately 60% drop in the pyruvate content (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by pyruvate measurement data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a showing reduced pyruvate levels in pfk2 knockdown larvae (p = 0.0497).

claim: Knockdown of pfk significantly decreased pyruvate levels.
source: Consistent with previous work (Li et al., 2018), knockdown of pfk significantly decreased pyruvate levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by pyruvate measurement data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a showing reduced pyruvate levels in pfk knockdown larvae (p = 0.0214), consistent with a cited previous study (Li et al., 2018).

claim: Knockdown of hex-A or hex-C had negligible effects on Hipk tumor growth.
source: Knockdown of hex-A or hex-C had negligible effects on Hipk tumor growth; as did hex-A and hex-C double knockdown (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy images in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a-c showing persistent tissue distortions in hipk-expressing discs with hex-A, hex-C, or double knockdown.

claim: Knockdown of glut1 or pgi failed to block Hipk-induced tumorigenesis.
source: Similarly, knockdown of glut1 or pgi failed to block Hipk-induced tumorigenesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 3a–b).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy images in Figure 6—figure supplement 3a-b showing persistent tissue distortions in hipk-expressing discs with glut1 or pgi knockdown.

claim: Flies ubiquitously depleted of pgk failed to reach the larval stage.
source: Likewise, we observed that flies ubiquitously depleted of pgk (act5c>pgk-RNAi) failed to reach the larval stage.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments showing lethality of pgk knockdown.

claim: Flies lacking pfk or pyk reached the larval stage but could not pupariate.
source: Flies lacking pfk (act5c>pfk-RNAi) or pyk (act5c>pyk-RNAi) reached the larval stage but could not pupariate.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments showing lethality of pfk or pyk knockdown at the larval-pupal transition.

claim: Flies with pfk2 knockdown died at the early pupal stage but did not differentiate further to become late pupae.
source: Flies with pfk2 knockdown (act5c>pfk2-RNAi) died at the early pupal stage but did not differentiate further to become late pupae.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments showing lethality of pfk2 knockdown at the early pupal stage.

claim: Most flies lacking glut1 or pgi succeeded in emerging as adults.
source: Most flies lacking glut1 (act5c>glut1-RNAi) or pgi (act5c>pgi-RNAi) succeeded in emerging as adults.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments showing that glut1 or pgi knockdown does not cause lethality.

claim: Otto Warburg first discovered that cancer cells vigorously take up glucose and preferentially produce lactate even in the presence of oxygen in the 1920s.
source: In the 1920s, Otto Warburg first discovered that cancer cells vigorously take up glucose and preferentially produce lactate even in the presence of oxygen, a phenomenon now widely termed the Warburg effect or aerobic glycolysis (Warburg et al., 1927).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to Warburg's original work (Warburg et al., 1927).

claim: The Warburg effect was largely disregarded for the decades following Warburg's discovery.
source: Despite his pioneering work, the Warburg effect was largely disregarded for the subsequent decades (Liberti and Locasale, 2016; Koppenol et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by citations (Liberti and Locasale, 2016; Koppenol et al., 2011).

claim: After the discoveries of oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, cancers are generally considered as genetic diseases rather than metabolic ones.
source: After the discoveries of oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, cancers are generally considered as genetic diseases rather than metabolic ones (Wishart, 2015; Seyfried et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the historical perspective on cancer supported by citations (Wishart, 2015; Seyfried et al., 2014).

claim: The revisiting of the Warburg effect in connection with oncogenes in the 1980s sparked substantial research in cancer metabolism.
source: Not until the 1980s did the revisiting of the Warburg effect in connection with oncogenes spark substantial research in cancer metabolism (Koppenol et al., 2011), laying the foundation for 2-deoxy-2-(18F)fluoro-D-glucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET) in clinical cancer diagnosis (Vander Heiden et al., 2009; Ben-Haim and Ell, 2008), recognition of metabolic reprogramming as a hallmark of cancer (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Ward and Thompson, 2012) and development of anti-cancer agents targeting aerobic glycolysis (Ganapathy-Kanniappan and Geschwind, 2013; Pelicano et al., 2006; Granchi and Minutolo, 2012).
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by multiple citations describing the impact of renewed interest in the Warburg effect.

claim: Warburg hypothesized that mitochondrial impairment is the cause of aerobic glycolysis and cancer.
source: Warburg hypothesized that mitochondrial impairment is the cause of aerobic glycolysis and cancer (Warburg, 1956), which has sparked much controversy among scientists (Senyilmaz and Teleman, 2015).
evidence: This is a historical statement about Warburg's hypothesis supported by citations (Warburg, 1956; Senyilmaz and Teleman, 2015).

claim: The current, widely-accepted view is that oncogenic drivers such as RAS, MYC, hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) and steroid receptor coactivators (SRCs) promote cancer cell proliferation and directly stimulate aerobic glycolysis through regulating transcriptional expression or catalytic activities of metabolic enzymes.
source: Contrary to his idea, the current, widely-accepted view is that oncogenic drivers such as RAS, MYC, hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) and steroid receptor coactivators (SRCs) promote cancer cell proliferation and directly stimulate aerobic glycolysis through regulating transcriptional expression or catalytic activities of metabolic enzymes (Koppenol et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the current scientific consensus supported by citation (Koppenol et al., 2011).

claim: Drosophila has proven to be a powerful genetic model organism for studying tumorigenesis in vivo largely due to high conservation of genes and signaling cascades between human and flies and reduced genetic redundancy.
source: Drosophila has proven to be a powerful genetic model organism for studying tumorigenesis in vivo largely due to high conservation of genes and signaling cascades between human and flies and reduced genetic redundancy (Gonzalez, 2013; Herranz and Cohen, 2017) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of Drosophila as a model organism supported by citations (Gonzalez, 2013; Herranz and Cohen, 2017).

claim: Elevation of Drosophila Hipk causes an in vivo tumor model characterized by tissue overgrowth, loss of epithelial integrity and invasion-like behaviors.
source: In a recent study, we showed that elevation of Drosophila Hipk causes an in vivo tumor model characterized by tissue overgrowth, loss of epithelial integrity and invasion-like behaviors (Blaquiere et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings from the authors' group supported by citation (Blaquiere et al., 2018).

claim: HIPK1 is highly expressed in breast cancer cell lines, colorectal cancer samples and oncogenically-transformed mouse embryo fibroblasts.
source: For example, HIPK1 is highly expressed in breast cancer cell lines, colorectal cancer samples and oncogenically-transformed mouse embryo fibroblasts (Kondo et al., 2003; Rey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about HIPK1 expression in cancers supported by citations (Kondo et al., 2003; Rey et al., 2013).

claim: HIPK2 is elevated in certain cancers including cervical cancers, pilocytic astrocytomas, colorectal cancer cells and in other proliferative diseases, such as thyroid follicular hyperplasia.
source: Also, HIPK2 is elevated in certain cancers including cervical cancers, pilocytic astrocytomas, colorectal cancer cells and in other proliferative diseases, such as thyroid follicular hyperplasia (Al-Beiti and Lu, 2008; Cheng et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2009; D'Orazi et al., 2006; Saul and Schmitz, 2013; Deshmukh et al., 2008; Lavra et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about HIPK2 expression in cancers supported by multiple citations.

claim: 2-NBDG is transported into cells through glucose transporters and phosphorylated by hexokinases.
source: Like D-glucose, 2-NBDG is transported into cells through glucose transporters and phosphorylated by hexokinases (Yoshioka et al., 1996; O'Neil et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about the biochemical properties of 2-NBDG supported by citations (Yoshioka et al., 1996; O'Neil et al., 2005).

claim: Due to the presence of the fluorescent amino group at the C-2 position, 2-NBDG-6-phosphate cannot proceed further through glycolysis and is consequently trapped within the cells.
source: However, due to the presence of the fluorescent amino group at the C-2 position, 2-NBDG-6-phosphate cannot proceed further through glycolysis and is consequently trapped within the cells, rendering it a probe for monitoring glucose uptake (O'Neil et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about the biochemical properties of 2-NBDG supported by citation (O'Neil et al., 2005).

claim: Overexpression of glut1 is sufficient to promote the accumulation of 2-NBDG.
source: For example, overexpression of glut1 (encoding Glucose transporter 1) is sufficient to promote the accumulation in 2-NBDG (Niccoli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the effect of glut1 overexpression supported by citation (Niccoli et al., 2016).

claim: Increased import of 2-NBDG is found in dMyc-expressing cells.
source: Increased import of 2-NBDG is also found in dMyc-expressing cells (de la Cova et al., 2014) and RasV12scrib−/− tumor cells (Katheder et al., 2017), indicating that such cells acquire enhanced glucose metabolism.
evidence: This is a statement about 2-NBDG uptake in dMyc-expressing cells supported by citation (de la Cova et al., 2014).

claim: Increased import of 2-NBDG is found in RasV12scrib−/− tumor cells.
source: Increased import of 2-NBDG is also found in dMyc-expressing cells (de la Cova et al., 2014) and RasV12scrib−/− tumor cells (Katheder et al., 2017), indicating that such cells acquire enhanced glucose metabolism.
evidence: This is a statement about 2-NBDG uptake in RasV12scrib−/− tumor cells supported by citation (Katheder et al., 2017).

claim: Hexokinases phosphorylate glucose to form glucose-6-phosphate (G6P), which is the first essentially irreversible step in glycolysis.
source: Hexokinases phosphorylate glucose to form glucose-6-phosphate (G6P), which is the first essentially irreversible step in glycolysis (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the function of hexokinases in glycolysis, as illustrated in Figure 2b.

claim: Pgi catalyzes the reversible conversion of G6P and fructose-6-phosphate.
source: Pgi catalyzes the reversible conversion of G6P and fructose-6-phosphate.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the function of Pgi in glycolysis.

claim: Pfk2 is a bifunctional enzyme that synthesizes fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6-BP).
source: Pfk2 is a bifunctional enzyme that synthesizes fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6-BP).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the function of Pfk2.

claim: F2,6-BP is a potent allosteric activator of Pfk, which governs the committed, second irreversible step in glycolysis.
source: F2,6-BP is a potent allosteric activator of Pfk, which governs the committed, second irreversible step in glycolysis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the regulatory role of F2,6-BP in glycolysis.

claim: Ldh favors the reduction of pyruvate to lactate, regenerating nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) such that glycolysis continues unabated.
source: Ldh, similar to LDHA in vertebrates (Rechsteiner, 1970), favors the reduction of pyruvate to lactate, regenerating nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) such that glycolysis continues unabated (Valvona et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the function of Ldh supported by citations (Rechsteiner, 1970; Valvona et al., 2016).

claim: dMyc/MYC plays a conserved role in upregulating glycolysis in vertebrates and Drosophila during normal development and in cancers.
source: In addition to growth control, dMyc/MYC plays a conserved role in upregulating glycolysis in vertebrates and Drosophila during normal development and in cancers (de la Cova et al., 2014; Gallant, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the conserved function of dMyc/MYC supported by citations (de la Cova et al., 2014; Gallant, 2013).

claim: Vertebrate PFK was shown to physically interact with TEAD factors to stimulate YAP/TAZ activity, thus promoting proliferation and malignancy in cancer cells.
source: For example, vertebrate PFK was shown to physically interact with TEAD factors to stimulate YAP/TAZ activity, thus promoting proliferation and malignancy in cancer cells (Enzo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about PFK function beyond metabolism supported by citation (Enzo et al., 2015).

claim: PFKFB4 phosphorylates and activates oncogenic SRC-3 to promote breast cancers through stimulating purine synthesis.
source: PFKFB4 (an isoform of PFK2) phosphorylates and activates oncogenic SRC-3 to promote breast cancers through stimulating purine synthesis (Dasgupta et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about PFKFB4 function beyond metabolism supported by citation (Dasgupta et al., 2018).

claim: MYC is generally considered 'undruggable' largely due to its nuclear localization, lack of an enzymatic 'active site', and indispensable roles during normal development.
source: Although MYC functions in cancer metabolism are widely recognized, MYC is generally considered 'undruggable' largely due to its nuclear localization, lack of an enzymatic 'active site', and indispensable roles during normal development (Soucek and Evan, 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges of targeting MYC therapeutically supported by citation (Soucek and Evan, 2010).

claim: The hinge region was coined a 'tumor hotspot' because of its unique epithelial cell architectures and high endogenous JAK/STAT signaling.
source: The region-specific susceptibility to tumorigenic stimuli has been previously described and the hinge region was coined a 'tumor hotspot' because of its unique epithelial cell architectures and high endogenous JAK/STAT signaling (Tamori et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the hinge region's susceptibility to tumorigenesis supported by citation (Tamori et al., 2016).

claim: Flies lacking pfk2 exhibited elevated levels of circulating glucose and reduced sugar tolerance.
source: A previous report shows that flies lacking pfk2 exhibited levels of circulating glucose and reduced sugar tolerance, providing a functional link between Pfk2 and glucose metabolism (Havula et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the metabolic phenotype of pfk2 mutants supported by citation (Havula et al., 2013).

claim: EGFR-driven tumors feature robust upregulation of Ldh among other glycolytic genes.
source: For instance, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-driven tumors, tumors with activated platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) receptor (Pvr) and tumors with polarity loss (such as scrib or dlg mutant tumors) feature robust upregulation of Ldh among other glycolytic genes (Wang et al., 2016; Eichenlaub et al., 2018; Bunker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about metabolic changes in EGFR-driven tumors supported by citations (Wang et al., 2016; Eichenlaub et al., 2018; Bunker et al., 2015).

claim: Tumors with activated PDGF/VEGF receptor (Pvr) feature robust upregulation of Ldh among other glycolytic genes.
source: For instance, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-driven tumors, tumors with activated platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) receptor (Pvr) and tumors with polarity loss (such as scrib or dlg mutant tumors) feature robust upregulation of Ldh among other glycolytic genes (Wang et al., 2016; Eichenlaub et al., 2018; Bunker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about metabolic changes in Pvr-activated tumors supported by citations (Wang et al., 2016; Eichenlaub et al., 2018; Bunker et al., 2015).

claim: Tumors with polarity loss (such as scrib or dlg mutant tumors) feature robust upregulation of Ldh among other glycolytic genes.
source: For instance, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-driven tumors, tumors with activated platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) receptor (Pvr) and tumors with polarity loss (such as scrib or dlg mutant tumors) feature robust upregulation of Ldh among other glycolytic genes (Wang et al., 2016; Eichenlaub et al., 2018; Bunker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about metabolic changes in polarity-deficient tumors supported by citations (Wang et al., 2016; Eichenlaub et al., 2018; Bunker et al., 2015).

claim: Depletion of Ldh was shown to reduce growth of EGFR-driven tumors but not tumors with polarity loss.
source: Depletion of Ldh was shown to reduce growth of EGFR-driven tumors but not tumors with polarity loss (Eichenlaub et al., 2018; Bunker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the differential requirement for Ldh in different tumor types supported by citations (Eichenlaub et al., 2018; Bunker et al., 2015).

claim: In RasV12scrib−/− tumors, elevated glucose uptake was evident.
source: In RasV12scrib−/− tumors, elevated glucose uptake was evident, but its significance was not evaluated (Katheder et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about metabolic changes in RasV12scrib−/− tumors supported by citation (Katheder et al., 2017).

claim: Genetically targeting individual signaling cascades failed to restrain Hipk tumor growth.
source: In our previous study, we found that genetically targeting individual signaling cascades failed to restrain Hipk tumor growth (Blaquiere et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings from the authors' group supported by citation (Blaquiere et al., 2018).

claim: Targeting Pfk2 may be a favorable, selective metabolic strategy in the treatment of cancers, especially those displaying ectopic MYC expression.
source: Given that Pfk2 is mis-expressed in tumor cells but not in normal cells (Figure 2a) and that dMyc accumulation is most sensitive to the Pfk2-Pfk mediated committed step of glycolysis specifically in tumor cells (Figure 6), targeting Pfk2 may be a favorable, selective metabolic strategy in the treatment of cancers, especially those displaying ectopic MYC expression.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic strategies inferred from the data showing that Pfk2 is upregulated in tumors and required for dMyc accumulation specifically in tumor cells.
